title: Barefoot Running: The Best Podcast Episode in History
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss barefoot running: the philosophy that humans evolved to run long distances barefoot, the history of running shoes (Fort Rock sandals, rubber soles, Wait Webster, Reebok's Joseph William Foster, air cushioning and Frank Rudy with Nike, gel heels, New Balance Trackster, Nike Waffle trainer), Christopher McDougall's book Born to Run and the Tarahumara runners, Daniel Lieberman's Harvard research on heel striking and loading rates, calluses in Kenyan runners, the risks of switching too fast, minimalist shoes and Vibram FiveFingers, and shoe drop. The episode drifts into tangents about Police Academy, Party Down, and softball. It closes with listener mail about Tricky, smart water tagging for BT Openreach, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to barefoot running
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of barefoot running and the idea that humans evolved to run long distances. They joke about running and walking, and discuss how the trend started.

segments.title: History of running shoes
segments.summary: The hosts trace the history of the sneaker and running shoe: the Fort Rock sandals, rubber soles attached to uppers attributed to Wait Webster in 1832, the origin of the word sneakers, British terms like plimsolls and trainers, Reebok's origins with Joseph William Foster and his 1852 running spikes, and 1970s cushioned shoes.

segments.title: Air and gel cushioning, New Balance and Nike, and the running boom
segments.summary: The hosts discuss gel heel cushioning from the 1980s, air cushioning credited to Frank Rudy and Nike, New Balance's 1960 Trackster, Nike's waffle shoe, and the 1970s jogging boom linked to Forrest Gump. Skeptics call cushioning a marketing scam, and running injuries have reportedly risen since the 1970s.

segments.title: Born to Run, Tarahumara runners, and Lieberman's study
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Christopher McDougall's book Born to Run (2010) and its paleo-style argument that modern running shoes cause injuries. They describe the Tarahumara runners at the Leadville Trail 100 and Daniel Lieberman's Harvard study, which together drew attention to barefoot running.

segments.title: Pronation, supination, and running injury claims
segments.summary: The hosts discuss claims that running shoes cause injuries, including the idea that eight of ten runners get injured each year, and biomechanical problems such as pronation and supination. Barefoot proponents argue that going barefoot can correct these problems.

segments.title: Digression on movies and TV
segments.summary: The hosts go off topic, discussing Police Academy, the show Party Down, Steve Guttenberg, Megan Mullally, Kristen Bell, and a Mark Maron interview with Martin Starr.

segments.title: Heel striking, midfoot running, and the feet's nerve endings
segments.summary: The hosts explain why heel striking is poor form and why running on the forefoot or midfoot feels more natural barefoot. They describe a running class Josh took that taught a forward-falling technique. Barefoot proponents say the feet's nerve endings give feedback that shoes block.

segments.title: Minimalist shoes, Vibram socks, and transitioning to barefoot running
segments.summary: The hosts describe minimalist shoes and Vibram FiveFingers toe socks, which Chuck had criticized. They discuss Lieberman's study of Kenyan runners who have thick calluses, the arch and Achilles spring mechanism, and the study by Peter Weyand's group at SMU on loading rate. They advise transitioning to barefoot running slowly, and note that one runner was sore for days after switching too fast.

segments.title: Shoe drop and wrap-up of barefoot running
segments.summary: The hosts discuss shoe drop, the height difference between heel and forefoot, and how modern running shoes have become leaner. They conclude that the science is not settled on the best way to run.

segments.title: Listener mail: Tricky, smart water, and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener Liam writes about the Tricky album Product of the Environment and the nitroglycerin safe-cracking story, and about SmartWater being used by BT Openreach to tag copper wire. The hosts sign off and give contact information.
